extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent attorneys/agents, and patent applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating claim definiteness, means‑plus‑function limitations (§112, ¶6) and written description/enablement (§112, ¶1) in patent specifications; explains when disclosed structure is sufficient or insufficient to avoid indefiniteness. Used by examiners and practitioners during claim construction and prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means‑plus‑function (§112, ¶6) requires disclosure of corresponding structure
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim limitation invokes §112, ¶6, the specification must disclose the corresponding structure, material, or acts that perform the recited function; merely stating known techniques or methods can be used is not a disclosure of structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis begins by determining whether the specification discloses corresponding structure, material, or acts in accordance with §112, ¶6. Examples: failure to disclose structure for a ‘control means’ or ‘game control means’ renders the claim indefinite. Anti‑pattern: bare statements that a standard microprocessor with 'appropriate programming' or that 'known techniques can be used' are sufficient — they are not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer‑implemented means need an algorithm to provide sufficient structure
rubrics_metrics.description: For computer‑implemented means‑plus‑function claims, the patentee must disclose an algorithm that transforms a general purpose computer into a special purpose computer to perform the disclosed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee may express the algorithm as a mathematical formula, in prose, a flow chart, or other understandable terms. Simply reciting 'software' or 'microprocessor with appropriate programming' without algorithmic detail is insufficient and constitutes impermissible pure functional claiming. (See Aristocrat, Finisar, Katz examples.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must 'clearly link or associate' disclosed structure to the claimed function
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not enough that one of ordinary skill could implement a structure; the written description itself must disclose sufficient structure and clearly link/associate that structure to the claimed function so a skilled artisan understands the bounds of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification links controllers/circuitry/ACM/software to the claimed function with descriptive detail, that can establish the necessary link (e.g., Telecordia shows controllers linked to monitoring). If the specification only restates outcomes or uses black‑box abstractions, the link is missing (e.g., Blackboard ACM as 'black box').

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Software' label alone is insufficient as corresponding structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure that merely identifies 'software' executed by a CPU, without describing the algorithm or means to accomplish the function, does not provide sufficient corresponding structure under §112, ¶6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner/practitioner should look for algorithmic disclosure (flowchart, pseudo‑code, equations) rather than generic references to software. Finisar is an example where only 'software' was disclosed and held insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure functional claiming of a general purpose computer is indefinite unless algorithm disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: Claiming a general purpose computer programmed to perform a specialized function without disclosing the internal structure (algorithm) runs afoul of the prohibition on purely functional claiming and renders the claim indefinite under §112, ¶2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The public notice function is implicated: without algorithmic disclosure, the public cannot tell the metes and bounds of the invention. Katz examples illustrate this risk when no algorithm for conditional coupling was disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: General purpose computer disclosure may suffice for purely structural, conventional functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the recited function is one that any general purpose computer can perform without special programming (e.g., storing data), disclosure of a general purpose computer with memory may be sufficient corresponding structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context matters: if the function requires specialized processing, an algorithm is required; if the function is coextensive with general computer structure (e.g., data storage), the general purpose computer disclosure can be adequate (see Katz storing data example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equations and detailed mathematical disclosure can satisfy §112, ¶6 when coupled with known algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification discloses particular equations and the detailed components of those equations, stating that 'known algorithms' can be used to solve them can satisfy the corresponding structure requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dossel illustrates that when the application provides specific equations and the necessary detail, reference to known mathematical techniques may be sufficient because the Dossel court used 'algorithm' in a narrow sense (particular mathematical operations known in the art). Examiner should assess whether the remaining steps are basic techniques known to skilled artisans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black‑box descriptions of outcomes are insufficient structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure that describes only the outcome or function (an 'outcome' abstraction) without describing how the outcome is achieved fails to disclose corresponding structure under §112, ¶6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Access control manager (ACM) described only as creating an access control list without describing how the ACM performs the assigning function is a black‑box and leads to indefiniteness. Look for structure that explains the means of achieving the outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not import unrecited functions from dependent claims into independent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The corresponding structure for a means‑plus‑function limitation should be limited to performing the recited function; one should not require disclosure of additional, unrecited functions (which may be recited in dependent claims) to support the independent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wenger example: 'circulating' is the recited function in claim 1; requiring structure for 'recirculating' (recited only in claim 3) would improperly import limitations. Examiner/practitioner must match structure to the specific recited function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must satisfy written description (§112, ¶1) by showing possession of claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: To meet the written description requirement, the specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art would reasonably conclude the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must describe the invention in a manner understandable to a person of ordinary skill and show the inventor actually invented the claimed subject matter. This is separate but related to §112, ¶6 analysis and impacts breadth of functional limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement (§112, ¶1) requires teaching how to make and use the full scope without undue experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must teach those skilled in the art how to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation to satisfy enablement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional claim limitations that cover all means/methods of performing a function can render a claim broader than the enabling disclosure and thus unsupported. Examiner/practitioner should evaluate whether enabling disclosure commensurates with claimed breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment is fact‑specific — examples can support or defeat indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether disclosure is sufficient is determined on facts: detailed embodiments, figures, controller circuitry, protocols (e.g., DDE) or equations can make a claim definite; generic or minimal disclosures can make it indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use case law examples (Aristocrat, Finisar, Katz, Wenger, Dossel, All Voice, Telecordia) to analogize facts. Look for detailed description, links between structure and function, algorithms/protocols, or accepted domain techniques to determine sufficiency.
